content_html:
Pattern Keeper is a PDF chart reader built specifically for cross stitch. On compatible patterns it can provide a continuous view across page breaks, search and highlight symbols, and mark crosses as completed.

The search becomes useful when it is translated into concrete decisions about scale, materials and workflow. This guide focuses on those decisions so the result is stitchable rather than merely attractive in an image.

What the app actually does

Devices and availability

As of September 2026, the official site still states that the app is available on Android and that iOS is not yet available. Anyone buying a device specifically for the app should check the current requirements in its FAQ.

PDF compatibility

Not every PDF imports with the same level of functionality. Pattern Keeper publishes supported-designer lists and explains that the complexity of PDF formatting prevents a universal compatibility guarantee.

Current limitations

The official FAQ says the app currently supports full cross stitches; backstitch and fractional stitches are still not interpreted as stitch types. Those elements need to be checked in the original PDF or another viewer.

What a designer should test

Recent WinStitch and MacStitch releases include a dedicated Pattern Keeper export. For designers, testing the actual exported file matters more than assuming compatibility because of the software used.

How to communicate compatibility

If we advertise compatibility, our PDFs need to be tested before that claim appears on a product page. A clear verified promise adds value; an assumed compatibility badge creates frustration.

The best solution is the one that keeps the project clear, achievable and consistent with the intended finish. The same standard should guide our catalogue: solve the stitcher's need first and let the technical quality of the pattern do the commercial work afterward.

Pattern Keeper is designed for reading and tracking cross-stitch charts rather than creating them. When a PDF imports well, the app can combine chart pages into a continuous working view, recognize symbols, highlight a selected symbol and mark completed stitches. Those functions are especially useful on large full-coverage charts because they reduce repeated scanning across printed pages.

Compatibility depends on how the PDF was built. A visually perfect PDF can still import poorly if the chart is stored as flattened images, uses unusual fonts or encodes the grid in ways the app cannot interpret. That is why “PDF” alone is not a compatibility guarantee. Before starting a large project, import the actual file and test symbol search, page alignment and the key rather than assuming every feature will work.

The original PDF still matters even when Pattern Keeper becomes the main working tool. Backstitch, fractional stitches, special instructions, materials and finishing notes may need to be read outside the interpreted chart. Keep the source file unchanged and use the app as a progress layer, not as a replacement for every piece of pattern information.

For designers, export quality should be tested on a real device. If our software can create a Pattern Keeper-friendly file, we should still open the exported PDF, verify symbol recognition and compare stitch coordinates with the master chart. A compatibility statement should be based on that test and version, not on the assumption that all PDFs from one program behave identically.

Digital tracking is most valuable when it preserves orientation. Clear ten-stitch grid lines, stable coordinates and sensible page boundaries make it easier to recover if annotations are lost or the file needs to be opened elsewhere. Those same qualities also improve printing, so designing for digital readers should not require sacrificing a strong conventional PDF.

For MAKE, Pattern Keeper compatibility can become a meaningful product feature on large charts, but only if we validate it. The product page should state what was tested and avoid promising support for stitch types the app does not interpret. A customer should know whether they can search full crosses digitally and where they still need to consult the original PDF.

File size and page construction also affect the experience on older tablets. A chart can be technically compatible and still feel slow if the PDF is extremely heavy. Designers should balance crisp symbols with efficient export and test zooming, highlighting and page movement on a realistic device rather than only on a desktop computer.

Progress data should be treated separately from the purchased master file. Keep a clean backup of the PDF and, where the app permits, back up progress according to its current options. Digital convenience is valuable, but a large project should not depend on one device containing the only usable copy.

Because app capabilities can change, any MAKE compatibility note should be dated or versioned. We can state that a file was tested successfully at publication without promising that every future app release will interpret it identically.
